title: Literal Types, as const, and satisfies
summary: Limit values to a fixed set with literal unions, derive types from data with as const, and check objects with satisfies without losing detail.
intro: Many values in real code come from a short, fixed list: a direction, an HTTP status, a plan name, a feature flag. TypeScript can type the list itself, so a typo like `"nort"` is a type error instead of a bug. In this lesson you build those types from literals, derive them from data you already have, and check configuration objects without losing their details.

steps.title: Literal unions
steps.body:
A literal type is one exact value used as a type, like `"north"`, `404`, or `true`. Join literals with `|` to say "one of these values":

```typescript types
type Direction = "north" | "south" | "east" | "west";
type HttpError = 400 | 404 | 500;
```

A `Direction` accepts those four strings and nothing else. Passing `"up"` is a type error (TS2345), and so is a `string` variable, because it could hold anything. A `const` holding `"north"` has the type `"north"`, so it fits. A `let` widens to `string` unless you annotate it: `let heading: Direction = "north"`.

A `switch` on a literal union handles one value per `case`. When every case returns, TypeScript knows the function always returns, so it needs no `default`.

A `Record` keyed by a union must have every key: `Record<Direction, string>` is an object with exactly those four properties. Leave one out and the checker names the missing key, which makes it a safe lookup table.

examples.title: Directions
examples.prompt: Move a point one step at a time with a switch over a union of four directions.
examples.explanation: `Direction` lists the four allowed strings, and `Direction[]` is an array that may only hold them. The `switch` has one `case` per member and every case returns, so `tsc` accepts `move` without a final `return`. Add a fifth direction to the union without a `case` for it, and `move` could end without returning a `Position`, which `tsc` reports as TS2366. At runtime `direction` is an ordinary string: the literal types are erased like every other type.

examples.title: A value not in the union
examples.prompt: Call move with a direction the union does not list.
examples.output: main.ts(8,18): error TS2345: Argument of type '"up"' is not assignable to parameter of type 'Direction'.
examples.explanation: `"up"` is a string, but not one of the four the union allows, so the call fails with TS2345, which names both types. Nothing runs, not even the valid first call, because a type error stops the whole program. In editors with TypeScript support, such as VS Code, typing `move("` lists the four directions as completions, so most of these mistakes never get typed at all.

examples.title: Number and boolean literals
examples.prompt: Name each face of a die with a lookup table keyed by a union of numbers, then require a literal true in a request.
examples.output:
3 is three
6 is six
1 is one
Yahtzee reset
examples.explanation: `Dice` is a union of six number literals, so `rolls` can only hold real faces, and a `7` in it would not compile. `FACES` is a `Record<Dice, string>`, so it must have all six keys, and since every key is guaranteed, `FACES[value]` is a plain `string`, never `undefined`. In `ResetRequest`, `confirmed: true` accepts only the literal `true`, so callers have to confirm on purpose: `confirmed: false` is a type error. The type `boolean` is itself the union `true | false`.

practice.title: Traffic light
practice.prompt:
Cycle a traffic light through its colors.

1. Make `Light` a union of `"red"`, `"yellow"`, and `"green"`.
2. Make `next` return the light that comes after its argument: red, then green, then yellow, then red again.

Expected output:

```text
red -> green
green -> yellow
yellow -> red
red -> green
```

tests.output:
red -> green
green -> yellow
yellow -> red
red -> green

cases.name: rejects a color that is not a light

hints: Write the union like `Direction` in the first example: the three strings joined with `|`.
A `switch` on `light` with one `case` per color, each returning the next color, needs no `default`.
If `tsc` reports TS2366, a color in the union has no `case` that returns.

steps.title: Deriving types with as const
steps.body:
Often the allowed values already exist as data, like a list you loop over. Put `as const` after an array or object literal to keep every literal type and make the whole value readonly, all the way down:

```typescript
const ROLES = ["admin", "editor", "viewer"] as const;
//    ^? const ROLES: readonly ["admin", "editor", "viewer"]
console.log(ROLES.join(", ")); // admin, editor, viewer
```

Without `as const`, `ROLES` would be a `string[]`. With it, `ROLES` is a readonly tuple of three literals, and you can derive the union from the data instead of writing the values twice:

- `typeof ROLES` in a type position means the type of the value `ROLES`.
- `[number]` after an array type means its element type, so `(typeof ROLES)[number]` is the union of the three roles.
- `keyof typeof HTTP` gives the keys of an object value, and `(typeof HTTP)[keyof typeof HTTP]` gives the union of its values.

Add a role to the array and the derived type follows. Despite the `as`, nothing is converted or forced: `as const` only asks TypeScript to infer the narrowest types it can.

examples.title: Roles from a list
examples.prompt: Derive a Role type from an as const array, then loop over the same array to print every role.
examples.output:
admin: can edit
editor: can edit
viewer: read only
examples.explanation: `ROLES` is a readonly tuple of three string literals, and `(typeof ROLES)[number]` reads its element type: the union in the bubble. The list exists once, as data you can loop over, and the type comes from it. In the loop, `role` already has the type `Role`, so it goes straight into `canEdit`. If `ROLES` were a plain `string[]`, `Role` would be `string` and `canEdit` would accept any text.

examples.title: Codes from an object
examples.prompt: Name HTTP status codes in an as const object, then derive the union of its keys and of its values.
examples.explanation: `as const` keeps `ok` as the literal `200` instead of widening it to `number`, and makes both properties readonly. `keyof typeof HTTP` is the union of the object's keys, and indexing the object's type with all of them gives the union of its values, `200 | 404`. So `describeStatus(500)` is a type error, while every code in `HTTP` is accepted, and callers can still write `HTTP.notFound` instead of a bare `404`.

examples.title: Deep readonly
examples.prompt: Try to add a role to the as const array.
examples.output: main.ts(3,7): error TS2339: Property 'push' does not exist on type 'readonly ["admin", "editor", "viewer"]'.

practice.title: Plan tiers
practice.prompt:
List subscription plans once, as data, and derive their type from it.

1. Add `as const` to `PLANS`.
2. Derive `Plan` from `PLANS`.
3. Make `priceFor` look the price up in a `Record<Plan, number>`: free is 0, pro is 12, and team is 30 dollars a month.

Expected output:

```text
free: $0/month
pro: $12/month
team: $30/month
```

cases.name: rejects a plan that is not listed
accepts a listed plan as a Plan

hints: `as const` goes right after the closing `]` of the array.
`(typeof PLANS)[number]` is the union of the array's elements, like `Role` in the first example.
Declare `const PRICES: Record<Plan, number> = { free: 0, pro: 12, team: 30 }` and return `PRICES[plan]`.

steps.title: Checking values with satisfies

examples.title: Routes
examples.prompt: Check a routes object with satisfies and read its known keys.

examples.title: Annotation versus satisfies
examples.prompt: Annotate the same routes as a Record and see what TypeScript forgets.
examples.explanation: With the annotation, `routes` is just a dictionary of strings. TypeScript no longer knows which keys exist, so `routes["blog"]` compiles, and every read, even of `about`, has the type `string | undefined`. Each read now needs a `??` or a check, and a typo in a key is no longer an error. `satisfies` keeps both the check and the known keys, which is why it suits objects like this.

examples.title: Catching a typo in config
examples.prompt: Misspell a key in a theme checked with satisfies.
examples.output: main.ts(8,3): error TS2561: Object literal may only specify known properties, but 'secondry' does not exist in type 'Theme'. Did you mean to write 'secondary'?
examples.explanation: `satisfies Theme` checks the object literal the way an annotation would, including the excess property check, so the misspelled `secondry` is reported with a suggestion (TS2561). Without `satisfies`, the object would compile, and the mistake would only show up later, as an error wherever some code reads `theme.secondary`.

practice.title: Feature flags
practice.prompt:
Keep a set of feature flags checked but precise, and list the ones that are on.

1. Check `flags` against `Record<string, boolean>` with `satisfies`.
2. Make `enabledFlags` return the names of the flags that are on, sorted alphabetically.

Expected output:

```text
Enabled: darkMode, newCheckout
```

cases.name: keeps the known flags as booleans
rejects a flag that does not exist

hints: Put `satisfies Record<string, boolean>` right after the object's closing brace, not as an annotation on `flags`.
`Object.entries(flags)` gives `[name, on]` pairs: keep the pairs that are on, then keep only the names.

recap:
- A literal type is one exact value: `"north"`, `404`, `true`. A union of literals, like `"red" | "green"`, allows only those values.
- A `switch` with a returning `case` for every member of a union needs no `default`.
- `Record<Union, V>` must have every key of the union, and reading a key gives `V`, never `undefined`.
- `as const` keeps literal types and makes arrays and objects readonly all the way down.
- `(typeof LIST)[number]` turns an `as const` array into a union, and `(typeof OBJ)[keyof typeof OBJ]` does the same for an object's values.
- An annotation makes a variable exactly its type. `satisfies` checks a value against a type and keeps the precise type, so known keys stay known and typos are still caught.
